clue.text: Get rid of the pony and trap ?

definitions.meaning: to turn someone out is to expel or evict them
a horse with its carriage and fittings, the whole equipage, is an old sense of the noun

explanation.walkthrough: The verb phrase 'turn out' (evict) and the old noun for a carriage with its horse share the same letters; the hyphen in the count shows the noun form.
explanation.definitionFit: Expelling someone is turning them out, and an equipage of horse and carriage was once called a turn-out.

clue.text: When it's unco late, the Scotsman is a pillar of strength

definitions.text: When it's unco late, the Scotsman is a pillar of strength

parts.words: When it's unco late, the Scotsman is a pillar of strength
parts.note: a Scot saying 'too late, man' in dialect sounds out the name of a column carved as a muscular male figure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unco' is Scots for very, so it is too late; a Scotsman would say 'tae late, mon', which sounds like the architectural term for a column carved as a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A telamon is a supporting column sculpted as a strong male figure, so literally a pillar of strength.

clue.text: Featuring the tip-up variety

parts.note: describes a facial feature, a nose whose tip turns upward

explanation.walkthrough: 'Featuring' points at facial features: the word describes a nose turned up at the tip.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived adjective describes a turned-up nose, the tip-tilted kind.

clue.text: Hot spots for the Archdeacon, so distressing

indicators.note: the two letters of 'so' make room for the cleric's title, standing in place around it
distressing suggests the little word is upset and jumbled

parts.note: an archdeacon is styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven

explanation.surface: An archdeacon finds hot spots very upsetting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is the container signal: the cleric's title stands within the jumbled little word. Venerable is the formal style of an archdeacon in the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovens are chambers heated for cooking, so places of great heat.

clue.text: Time to get up, so yield to circumstances

parts.note: tempo is musical time or pace
to rise is to get up

explanation.surface: It's time to get up, so bow to the situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' and 'so' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To temporise is to stall and adapt one's conduct to the moment rather than act decisively.

clue.text: Spread out the notes of hand, boring as it is !

parts.note: to ted is to spread out mown hay to dry
a note of hand is a written promise to pay, an IOU, so several are IOUS

explanation.surface: A grumble about having to lay out a pile of promissory notes, a dull job.
explanation.walkthrough: TED is a farming verb: you ted hay by scattering it. 'as it is' just rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tedious is wearisome and dull, a plain synonym of boring.

clue.text: Trees should be very compactly arranged

definitions.note: the adverb phrase stands for the adjective, as in writing put very compactly

indicators.note: arranged tells us the letters of the trees are set out in another order

explanation.surface: Trees ought to be planted close together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges TREES. 'should be' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse writing uses few words, concise and brief.

clue.text: Girls in the Guards ?

parts.note: the young women whom protective fathers watch over and keep in their charge

explanation.walkthrough: 'the Guards' looks like a regiment; read it instead as the people guarding, the protective parents who keep watch over their girls.
explanation.definitionFit: A father's female children are girls under his guardianship.

clue.text: Wickerwork bed ?

parts.note: not a woven bed but a plantation of the willow used for basket-making

explanation.walkthrough: A bed of willows grown for basketry: 'bed' is a planting, not furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: The basket willow whose shoots make wicker is grown in beds named after it.

clue.text: Just the place for tasty sausages

definitions.text: Just the place for tasty sausages

parts.words: Just the place for tasty sausages
parts.note: a Greek island, site of a famous naval battle, whose name is also the plural of a spicy Italian sausage

explanation.walkthrough: The island of Salamis, where the Greeks beat the Persian fleet in 480 BC, has the same spelling as the plural of salami.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek island bears this name, which also spells the plural of a cured spicy sausage.

clue.text: The French and 'English can give us a turn

parts.note: la is the feminine form of 'the' in French
the English word for the article is simply 'the'

explanation.surface: A remark that combining French and English might produce a twist of some sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' is translated twice: LA in French, THE in English. 'give us a turn' is not a fright but what a lathe does, spinning work to shape it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lathe is a machine that rotates a workpiece while it is shaped, so it gives a turn.

clue.text: Like that flighty messenger from Olympus

definitions.text: Like that flighty messenger from Olympus

parts.words: Like that flighty messenger from Olympus
parts.note: the Roman messenger god with winged feet, whose name also gives the adjective for a volatile, changeable temperament

explanation.walkthrough: The god Mercury, swift messenger of the gods, lends his name both to quicksilver and to the adjective for a lively, unpredictable person.
explanation.definitionFit: A mercurial person is volatile and fickle, like the winged messenger god the word comes from.

clue.text: Literary masterpiece recovered by astronauts

definitions.meaning: Wilkie Collins's 1868 detective novel, often called the first great English detective story
lunar rock brought back by the Apollo crews would be stone from the moon

explanation.walkthrough: The Wilkie Collins novel 'The Moonstone' doubles as a description of the rock samples Apollo astronauts brought home.
explanation.definitionFit: Collins's classic novel carries this title, and a rock gathered on the lunar surface is literally a stone from the moon.

clue.text: Barchester Hospital founder

parts.note: in Trollope's novel The Warden the almshouse in Barchester was endowed by a wool-stapler named John, whose surname it bears

explanation.walkthrough: Trollope's 'The Warden' turns on the charity called Hiram's Hospital, left by John Hiram for twelve old men of Barchester.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's Barchester almshouse was endowed by the wool-stapler John Hiram and carries his name.

clue.text: Business intruders

parts.note: people who poke their faces into other folk's affairs are said to stick them in where they are not wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Business' reads like commerce, but the idiom is poking one's nose into someone else's business.
explanation.definitionFit: To nose into someone's business is to pry, so these facial features are the organs that intrude.

clue.text: The Elsinore ghost was so completely armoured

definitions.text: The Elsinore ghost was so completely armoured

parts.words: The Elsinore ghost was so completely armoured
parts.note: Hamlet's father's ghost appears at Elsinore armed from head to foot in metal plate

explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet the ghost appears on the Elsinore battlements 'armed at point exactly, cap-a-pe', fully covered in metal armour.
explanation.definitionFit: Clad in steel means wearing metal plate armour from head to foot.

clue.text: Entrances the French painter going east in the vessel

parts.note: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was a French Neoclassical painter

indicators.note: the east letter is placed inside the ship abbreviation

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A French artist sailing eastward aboard a ship and making his entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrances' looks like a verb meaning enchants, but it is the plural noun: ways in. 'going' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingress is an act or way of entering, so ingresses are entrances.

clue.text: Shown by a fighting M.P.?

parts.note: an MP with military service is addressed in the Commons as 'the honourable and gallant member', so the quality is shown by him

explanation.walkthrough: In the House of Commons an MP who has served in the forces was traditionally called 'the honourable and gallant member'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallantry is bravery, the quality behind the Commons title for an MP who served in the armed forces.

clue.text: Not the napery for the' upper crust

definitions.text: Not the napery for the' upper crust

parts.words: Not the napery for the' upper crust
parts.note: the table cloth word that the upper class avoid, a classic 'non-U' term

explanation.walkthrough: Nancy Mitford's U and non-U lists said the upper class say 'napkin'; the French-derived word is the genteel middle-class choice.
explanation.definitionFit: This word for a table napkin was branded non-U, a term the upper class would never use.

clue.text: A bit at a time is not sound warfare

definitions.meaning: throwing forces into battle in dribs and drabs rather than together is a classic military error

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense trades on 'piecemeal attacks', committing troops in small packets, which military writers condemn.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in separate portions is the plain meaning, and committing troops in bits is condemned strategy.

clue.text: Interrogate the family re Peter's diet

parts.note: to pump someone is to question them persistently
kin means family

explanation.surface: Grilling the relatives about what Peter eats.
explanation.walkthrough: 're' is a link. The nursery rhyme 'Peter, Peter, pumpkin eater' gives Peter's food.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme Peter is a pumpkin eater, so the vegetable is his food.

clue.text: Cupid's missiles in reverse hit a short Cremona notability

indicators.note: in reverse tells us to read the word for the love god's arrows backwards

parts.note: Cupid shoots darts or arrows of love

explanation.surface: Cupid's arrows strike a violin from Cremona backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Cremona in Italy was home to Stradivari; his violins are Stradivarius, shortened to Strad. 'hit' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stradivarius violin, made in Cremona, is a celebrated instrument and commonly abbreviated.

clue.text: Pudding addicts are old sillies

definitions.meaning: duff is a boiled pudding, so people who love it would be duff fans
incompetent or stupid people, often elderly

explanation.walkthrough: Duff is a stodgy boiled pudding, as in plum duff, so the first sense treats the word as 'duff-ers', fans of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumbling incompetent is called a duffer, and the word also builds on duff, a boiled pudding.

clue.text: Just the one to display fashion at fifty

parts.note: mode means fashion or style
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A mannequin showing off clothes at the age of fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' places MODE next to L. The definition borrows the surface: a model is the person employed to display clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashion model is employed to show off clothes, so she is the one who displays them.

clue.text: Twill do for jeans

parts.note: read as 'it will serve for jeans', but also a twill cloth that serves for jeans

explanation.walkthrough: 'Twill' is both the contraction ''twill' (it will) and the diagonal-weave cloth; the cotton twill used for jeans answers both readings.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard-wearing cotton twill is the standard material for jeans.

clue.text: Suitor in an ugly quarrel.

parts.note: plain means unattractive
a tiff is a petty quarrel

explanation.surface: A suitor caught up in a nasty row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suitor' suggests a wooer, but here it is one who brings a lawsuit. 'in an' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaintiff brings a suit in court, so is literally one who sues.

clue.text: Outcome of E. A going on writing

indicators.note: in a down answer the poet goes on top of the writing

parts.note: E. A. are the initials of Edgar Allan Poe
MS is short for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: The result of E. A. continuing to write.
explanation.walkthrough: 'E. A.' points to the American writer Edgar Allan Poe; his surname sits above MS, the manuscript.
explanation.definitionFit: Poems are the output of a poet's labour, the work produced.

clue.text: Just the stuff for short transatlantic terminals

parts.note: New York, abbreviated NY, is one end of the Atlantic crossing
London, abbreviated LON, is the other end

explanation.surface: The ideal material for brief flights across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: The two cities at each end of the Atlantic run, New York and London, are abbreviated. 'stuff' means fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fabric, and 'stuff' is an old word for woven material.

clue.text: "And-creature in'ould Donegal " (Graves)

parts.note: a missing superlative from a song lyric by the Irish poet Alfred Perceval Graves, praising the gentlest girl in old Donegal

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the dash stands for the missing word in Graves's Irish song, meaning the most gentle and good-natured.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of a word for gentle and warm-hearted fills the gap in the Irish lyric.

clue.text: No recollection of the river

definitions.meaning: in Greek myth, the river of the underworld whose waters made the dead forget

explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the dead drank from this underworld river to forget their past lives, so its name means oblivion.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythic underworld stream brought oblivion, and its name became a word for forgetfulness.

clue.text: A demon's at large among the travellers

indicators.note: at large means roaming free, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A fiend roams loose among a band of wanderers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at large' rearranges A DEMONS. The answer is an old form of nomads, people who roam without a fixed home.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomads are wandering peoples who move from place to place, so they are travellers.

clue.text: Statesmen look for negative return

indicators.note: return asks us to read the whole run of seeking and refusing backwards

parts.note: to seek is to look for
nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: Politicians hunting for a rejection to come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reverses SEEK + NAY together to give YAN + KEES. 'Statesmen' means men of the States, Americans, not politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans, people from the United States, are colloquially called Yankees.
